explanation: Both models fail on this complex multi-block table (real-estate price comparisons). Qwen merges cell values within rows (e.g., 'this listing $744 || this listing is...') instead of separating each space-delimited token into its own column. T5Gemma correctly uses '||' delimiters and gets cell values right, but is likely penalized for trailing whitespace or column-count inconsistencies across the irregular blocks, or for wrapping the JSON in markdown code fences (```json). The table has an unusual jagged structure with metadata rows that shift column counts, making consistent segmentation extremely difficult for both models.

Both models make the same error: 'Bethel College Mishawaka' (a single institution name that includes the city) is incorrectly split into 'Bethel College||Mishawaka||Mishawaka||Masters||2,097', adding an extra column. This error propagates through the row and breaks the expected 4-column schema. All other rows appear correctly parsed, so the failure is a single token-boundary reasoning error on an ambiguous entry where the city name coincidentally matches a data field value.

T5Gemma correctly identifies that '10510 N Silverlake Pt' is a single address field and keeps the full address together as the first column. Qwen incorrectly splits the address on the internal space, outputting '10510||N Silverlake Pt||...' which breaks the column alignment for address rows. T5Gemma's tendency to be more conservative with delimiter insertion pays off here for these space-delimited address strings.

The label treats '14162 SW 260 ST 103' as a single address field. T5Gemma correctly keeps this as one field, but Qwen wrongly splits '14162 SW 260 ST' and '103' into separate columns for the first row. However, both models appear to fail for different or related reasons — T5Gemma's output appears mostly correct for the first row but may differ in trailing rows or other edge cases. The shared failure likely involves column-count consistency issues across the 23-row table where some entries have ambiguous field boundaries.

The only difference is how the models handle Spanish special characters. T5Gemma preserves the original UTF-8 characters (e.g., '1ª Ronda', 'Subcampeón') exactly as in the label. Qwen converts them to Unicode escape sequences or substitutes characters (e.g., '1\u00b0 Ronda' for '1ª Ronda', 'Subcampe\u00f3n' for 'Subcampeón'), which causes a mismatch during exact-match evaluation. The structural parsing is otherwise identical between both models.

The label format is '2.||YOUWATCH||The English Teacher||Ajouté par R00T le 19/10/2013' — four columns where the row number with period is in column 1 and the full attribution phrase is kept together in column 4. Qwen uses spaces around delimiters ('2. || YOUWATCH || ...') and keeps the attribution together correctly, but fails on whitespace format. T5Gemma merges the row number with the platform name ('2. YOUWATCH||...') losing the row-number column, and wrongly splits the attribution phrase ('Ajouté par R00T||le 19/10/2013'). Both fail differently: Qwen on delimiter whitespace, T5Gemma on structural column identification.

Both models correctly parse all six rows with the right values and column boundaries. The only minor difference is Qwen uses spaces around delimiters (' || ') while T5Gemma uses compact '||' without spaces; both appear to be accepted by the evaluator. T5Gemma wraps in markdown code fences (```json) but the evaluator still accepts it.

Both models produce identical outputs, correctly parsing the date-range rows with HTML entity values (€). No differences in approach; both models handle the n/a values and the date range strings in column 1 correctly.

Both models make the same segmentation error: they collapse the 'Championship/Event', 'Style', and 'Category' columns into a single merged field (e.g., 'World Championship Freestyle Seniors' as one column instead of three). The label expects these to be separate columns. Since both models produce identical wrong output, this appears to be a shared reasoning failure caused by the absence of clear field separators between multi-word event names and category labels.

Both models correctly handle the football club/season statistics table. Values and column counts are aligned with the label. T5Gemma adds markdown code fences but the evaluator still accepts it. No notable differences in approach.

The label expects the rank number and team name to be separate columns (e.g., '2||Liverpool||...'). Qwen uses spaces around delimiters ('2 || Liverpool ||') which likely fails exact matching. T5Gemma merges rank number with team name as a single field ('2 Liverpool||...'), losing the rank column entirely. Both fail to correctly segment the leading rank number from the team name, but via different mechanisms.

Similar to idx 91, the label expects the score to be kept as a single compound field ('4 - 0' as one value) while both models split the score into three separate columns ('4 || - || 0' or '4||-||0'). Qwen also uses spaces around delimiters. T5Gemma correctly uses compact delimiters but still splits the score field. Both models fail to recognize that '4 - 0' is a single atomic score string.

The label treats the multi-currency weekly rate ('€ 504US$ 680GB£ 424') as a single cell value. T5Gemma correctly keeps all currency values concatenated within a single column. Qwen incorrectly splits the three currency values into separate columns ('€ 504||US$ 680||GB£ 424 Get instant quote'), misidentifying the column boundaries and over-segmenting the rate field.

The label includes trailing empty columns (e.g., 'US Size||US2||...||US16||||||||||||||||') which neither model reproduces correctly. Qwen additionally uses spaces around delimiters and escapes HTML entities incorrectly ('\\u0026frac12;' vs '½'). T5Gemma handles HTML entities correctly but drops the trailing empty padding columns for the size-category rows. Both fail due to missing trailing empty column delimiters that preserve a fixed column count across rows.

Both models produce outputs that appear visually correct, with consistent 3-column formatting (Name||Role||Salary). Given the long list of names, the likely failure mode is truncation: the model outputs are cut off before reproducing the full list of rows, causing an incomplete match against the full label. Qwen uses spaces around delimiters which would also cause a mismatch.

The label keeps the deficiency type as a single compound phrase (e.g., 'Pharmacy Service Deficiencies'). T5Gemma correctly preserves these compound phrases as single column values. Qwen incorrectly splits each compound phrase into two columns ('Pharmacy||Service||Deficiencies' instead of 'Pharmacy Service Deficiencies'), over-segmenting multi-word field values and producing more columns than expected.

This table has sparse data with many empty cells represented as blank spaces, making column boundary detection especially difficult. Qwen collapses multiple columns into merged text blobs after the first two columns ('Angola || 6 || 5 - 4 || 4 - 4 - -'). T5Gemma also merges the country name with the first numeric value ('Angola 6||5||...') and leaves trailing whitespace within cells. Neither model can reliably infer column count from the irregular whitespace pattern of blank cells.

The first row of the label is '||%||%||%||%||%||%' — an empty first column followed by six '%' columns. Qwen uses single-pipe '|' delimiters instead of '||', and also drops the leading empty column. T5Gemma splits the date strings into components ('2011||Oct||6-9||...') instead of keeping '2011 Oct 6-9' as a single compound date field, and renders the header row as a single undelimited string. Both models fail the header row and at least one other structural requirement.

Both models correctly reconstruct the 5-row soccer statistics table with all 12 columns. The label includes a header row which both models reproduce faithfully. T5Gemma wraps in markdown fences but the evaluator accepts it. No notable differences in approach.

Both models produce identical outputs that merge the postal code and city into a single column ('3400 Klosterneuburg') instead of keeping them as separate columns as the label requires ('3400||Klosterneuburg'). This is a consistent shared error — both models treat the 4-digit code and city name as a single address component rather than two separate fields.

The label expects '- ' and the bath count as separate columns (e.g., '||-||1||'). T5Gemma merges the '-' placeholder and the bath count into a single field ('- 1', '- 2', '- 1.5') without inserting a delimiter between them, collapsing two columns into one. Qwen correctly identifies the '-' as a standalone column and the bath count as its own column, maintaining the proper 8-column structure throughout.

Both models correctly handle the torrent tracker URL table with 6 columns. Qwen produces compact '||' delimiters without spaces, matching the label exactly. T5Gemma uses ' || ' with surrounding spaces for the empty '-' cells, which still passes evaluation. Both models correctly preserve the URL strings as single atomic values.

The label has rows with empty middle columns preserved as '||||||' (e.g., 'christmas & new year||christmas & new year||...||7 nights||£250||||£1,250'). Qwen almost matches but drops or misplaces the empty column for 'christmas & new year' row (' £1,250' with a leading space instead of '||£1,250'). T5Gemma drops the empty columns entirely for rows like 'half term' and 'easter', merging fields across what should be empty placeholder columns. Both fail to correctly preserve the empty-column structure.

Qwen correctly separates all fields using '||' delimiters with spaces, matching the label. T5Gemma merges the first row label 'Power Supply' with the value 'AC' into a single cell ('Power Supply AC||...'), losing the column boundary between the feature name and its first data column. This collapses the row from 6 to 5 columns for that first row only, but is sufficient to cause a mismatch.

The label keeps the rank and team name together as a single first-column value (e.g., '10. Newcastle||...'). T5Gemma correctly keeps '10. Newcastle' as one field. Qwen splits the rank number from the team name into two separate columns ('10.||Newcastle||...'), adding an extra column and breaking the 7-column schema. This is the same rank-splitting error seen in idx 91, but here only Qwen makes it while T5Gemma avoids it.

The label keeps 'N. Backstrom C' as a single compound first-column value (player name + position). Both models split this into two columns: 'N. Backstrom||C||...' and 'N. Backstrom || C || ...' respectively. This structural split consistently affects every player row and creates an off-by-one column misalignment throughout the entire table. Both models make the same segmentation error, treating the position abbreviation as a separate column.
